lines.text: Your crops are dying, but the river runs below your fields.
So you haul water up the bank in buckets, one heavy trip at a time.
But by sunset, you've barely watered a single row.
So you cut a long log, round it smooth, and mark each end into eight equal parts.
You soak thin willow strips in pitch and wind them around the log in a slanted spiral.
Layer after layer, they build up into eight twisting blades. This is a helix.
But water just slides right off the open blades.
So you wrap it in planks, seal the seams with pitch, and bind it with iron hoops.
Now it's a closed wooden tube with a spiral inside.
You set the bottom in the river and tip it up, three feet high for every five feet long.
But it just sits there, and nothing moves.
So you put an iron pin in each end, rest them on a frame, and fix a handle to the top. This is a crank.
You turn it, and the low end scoops up water, trapping a pocket between the blades.
With every turn, the pockets climb the spiral, and water pours out the top. This is an Archimedes screw.
But some water leaks back down past the blades.
That's fine. The pocket below catches it and carries it up again.
So you dig a channel from the top of the screw out to your fields.
Now the river flows uphill, and people will use this trick for over two thousand years.
Congratulations. You have built an Archimedes screw.
